analysis.one_liner: Requires millionaires to pay at least 30% of their income in federal taxes.
analysis.headline: A bill requiring millionaires to pay a 30% minimum tax rate died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require people whose income tops $1 million a year to pay at least 30% of that income in federal taxes, after deducting charitable giving. Any amount they owe above their current income tax, minimum tax, and payroll tax would go to the Treasury, reducing the deficit. The bill also states the House's view that Congress should close tax loopholes that let the wealthiest pay less.
analysis.who_benefits: The federal Treasury and, indirectly, everyone who shares the burden of the national debt, because the bill is written specifically to reduce the deficit by taxing high incomes more [S3]. Ordinary taxpayers would also face a tax code in which the highest earners cannot pay an effective rate far below the middle-class rate, and low- and middle-income households would pay nothing extra since the tax only applies above $1 million of income [S2].

how_it_helps.text: It sets a floor: anyone with income over $1 million would owe at least 30% of income above their charitable contributions, closing the gap that lets some very high earners pay effective rates below middle-income families [S2][S3].
It raises revenue from the top of the income distribution specifically to reduce the federal deficit, rather than cutting spending or raising taxes on anyone else [S3].

The tax phases in gradually for incomes just above $1 million, and the $1 million threshold rises with inflation after 2016, so it targets the very top rather than catching more people over time [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Households with adjusted gross income over $1 million, who would owe the difference between a 30% minimum tax and their current tax bill; some itemizers would also lose part of their charitable contribution deduction at high incomes.

drawbacks.text: The bill concedes that its 30% minimum is an 'interim step' rather than full reform, and it does not close the specific loopholes, such as low rates on investment income, that create the gap in the first place [S3].
It adds a parallel tax calculation on top of the existing alternative minimum tax, making the tax code more complicated for high-income filers and the IRS [S3].
By reducing the value of charitable deductions for millionaires, it could shrink high-end charitable giving, which nonprofits rely on [S3].

The revenue would cut the deficit only by billions of dollars a year against annual deficits well over $400 billion at the time, so it would not by itself meaningfully change the nation's fiscal picture [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is fairness at the very top plus deficit reduction paid for entirely by households earning over $1 million; the costs are added tax complexity, a partial loss of charitable deduction value for large donors, and only modest deficit relief relative to the total deficit. The design is targeted and includes a phase-in and inflation adjustment, but it is a narrow fix rather than the broader tax reform its own language calls for. The larger story is that the bill never got a hearing, so none of these effects were ever tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there until Congress ended, never getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 14, 2015 with 21 cosponsors, all Democrats, and referred the same day to the Ways and Means Committee, which writes tax law [S3][S5].
The committee's only recorded action was the referral itself; no hearing, markup, or vote is listed in the two years before Congress ended [S5].
Because the bill never reached the House floor, the House never voted on the 30% minimum tax for millionaires [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning over $1 million a year, which would have owed the new minimum tax, are better off because the bill never moved. The committee's inaction also left existing deductions and lower effective rates for high earners untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Households earning over $1 million a year

industries.industry: High-income households and top earners ($1 million+)
industries.note: The bill's 30% minimum applies directly to households with adjusted gross income over $1 million, most of whose income often comes from investments and business ownership taxed at lower rates than wages. It would raise their effective federal tax rate toward the rates ordinary wage earners face.

industries.industry: Private equity, hedge funds, and investment managers
industries.note: Managers whose pay comes as carried interest and capital gains taxed below ordinary rates would face the largest increases under a 30% minimum on income over $1 million. The bill also counts existing payroll taxes toward the minimum, limiting only income-tax avoidance, not closing the carried-interest break itself.

The bill preserves a portion of the charitable contribution deduction for millionaires (the 'modified charitable contribution deduction') rather than eliminating it, so high-income giving keeps partial tax advantage. The phase-in also softens the initial hit.
